paras: The whipping of Henry Seay was a night attack in August 1880 on an elderly Black farmhand in the eastern part of Hickman County, in which unnamed men took him from his cabin, whipped him and ordered him to leave the neighborhood. Seay refused to go, and warrants were issued for one or two of the men, whom he had identified. The only account found is a special dispatch in the Chicago Daily Tribune, which called it "a dastardly outrage."

Shortly before the attack, Lindsey Berry had hired Seay, described as "an old negro man," to stay at his place, "the old Lumsden farm," feeding stock and doing chores for Berry's wife. Berry himself was away working on the Mobile Railroad extension near Columbus. According to the dispatch, "the employment of the old negro, and carrying him to the neighborhood, gave offense" to some local men.

One night, "without warning or warrant of excuse," these men went to Seay's cabin near the Berry house, took him out, whipped him, "treated him otherwise cruelly and brutally," and ordered him to leave. Hearing the attack, Mrs. Berry left her house and ran half a mile through the fields to a neighbor's, where she stayed. Once released, Seay went back into his cabin and remained there, "refusing to leave," and the attackers left without returning.

On the following Saturday "the necessary papers were issued," and an officer was sent after one or two of the men, who were known to Seay and reported by him. No report of an arrest, hearing or trial was found.

The Chicago Daily Tribune printed the story on August 28, 1880, as a special dispatch headed "OUTRAGE ON A NEGRO," on a page that also carried legal hangings in Texas and a Georgia report headlined "KU-KLUXED THE WRONG NEGRO." The surviving text has no dateline and ends with a closing quotation mark, suggesting the Tribune's correspondent was quoting a local paper. Its language condemned the attackers, calling them Seay's "tormentors" and the attack "dastardly."
No other white or Black paper was found to have carried the story.
